<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A model of teleseismic signal and surface-mode noise is derived from wave-propagation theory. Optimum Wiener multichannel frequency domain filters are designed to operate on the outputs of six seismometer arrays so as to pass signals and reject noise. The arrays studied include two 19-element surface arrays, two 19-element shallow-buried arrays and two 6-element vertical arrays where a 20-db reduction in spatially uncorrelated noise is assumed to result from seismometer burial. It is found that there is very little difference among the outputs of the filter systems designed for the two surface arrays and the two vertical arrays. The performance of the systems designed for the shallow-buried arrays is found to be considerably better. For one particular array, the predicted signal-to-noise improvement resulting from the assumed effect of shallow burial varies from 5 to 15 db.The theoretical results are sensitive to the amount of uncorrelated noise assumed in the model. However, when the levels of incoherent noise are equal, it appears that a surface array will generally possess greater capability for rejection of coherent noise than will a vertical array with the same size and number of receivers.The performance of an array of either type appears to be quite insensitive to changes of geometry if the number of receivers and the maximum dimension are not changed very much. Although a vertical array will always be superior to a single deeply buried seismometer, the improvement in performance which may be obtained by increasing the number of receivers in a vertical array is much less than in the case of a surface array.</jats:p>
title: Horizontal and vertical arrays for teleseismic signal enhancement

items.abstract: A Theory of Magnitude (AToM) (Walsh, 2003; Walsh, 2014) attempts to explain avisuo-spatial bias observed across magnitude processing domains (e.g., numerical, temporal).It proposes a generalised processing system which maps mental representations onto spacewith magnitude increasing with rightwards and upwards perceptions. As early findingssuggest linguistic magnitude processing may have an AToM consistent horizonal spatial bias(Myachykov et al., 2020), AToM would suggest a similar vertical spatial bias should beobserved in linguistic magnitude, wherein upwards space is associated with processing largermagnitudes. This study utilised random word generation upon alternating upwards anddownward head nods to assess the presence of a vertical spatial bias in the magnitude ofrandomly accessed linguistic representations. Participants each produced 50 random Englishwords resulting in a dataset of 2650 words. Syllabic Length, Semantic Size, Plurality andCountability were analysed as proxies for linguistic magnitude. Results found vertical NodDirection was not associated with any linguistic magnitude measure. These findings fail tosupport AToM’s prediction of a vertical spatial bias in the magnitude of randomly accessedlinguistic representations. Further research approaches aiming to explore both a verticalspatial component of linguistic magnitude processing and cross-domain interactions betweenlinguistic, spatial and other magnitude processing are suggested to further evaluate howsuccessfully AToM explains linguistic magnitude processing.
title: Horizontal Spatial Bias in the Magnitude of Freely Generated Words Failed to Replicate in the Vertical Axis

items.abstract: <jats:p>Ship-radiated noise exhibits horizontal directivity, but estimating the aspect-dependent characteristics of a ship of opportunity in shallow waters remains challenging owing to multipath interference. To quantitatively estimate this directivity, the relative radiation pattern was reconstructed using kilometer-scale measurements, and the absolute source level was estimated using data acquired at a closest-approach range of 240 m and an aspect angle of 60°. For the relative pattern reconstruction, array-averaged received levels from two 16-element vertical line arrays were compensated using transmission loss fitted to range-dependent variation over a constant-aspect reference segment. For the absolute source level estimation, the 240 m data were analyzed using ray-based blind deconvolution (RBD) and modeled Green’s functions. In the 200–900 Hz band, the relative source level toward the bow aspect was ~10 dB lower than that toward the broadside aspect, exhibiting a cardioid-like horizontal radiation pattern. In one-third octave bands, this pattern was not evident at 200 Hz. To provide an absolute reference for this pattern, the RBD analysis yielded a 200–900 Hz absolute source level of 169 dB at a 60° aspect angle. The findings suggest that considering directional characteristics can reduce aspect-related uncertainty in source level estimation, passive localization, and tracking.</jats:p>
title: Horizontal Directivity Estimation of Operational Ship-Radiated Noise Using Vertical Line Arrays in a Shallow-Water Waveguide

items.abstract: <jats:p>When shallow water internal waves approach a source-receiver track, the interference between the direct and horizontally refracted acoustic paths from a broadband acoustic source was previously shown to form Horizontal Lloyd’s mirror (Badiey et al. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 128(4), EL141–EL147, 2011). While the modal interference structure in the vertical plane may reveal arrival time for the out of plane refracted acoustic wave front, analysis of moving interference pattern along the horizontal array allows measurement of the angle of horizontal refraction and the speed of the nonlinear internal wave (NIW) in the horizontal plane. In this paper we present a full account of the movement of NIW towards a source-receive track and how we can use the received acoustic signal on an L-shaped array to estimate basic parameters of the waveguide and obtain related temporal and spatial coherence functions particularly in the vicinity of the formation of the horizontal Lloyd mirror. Numerical results using Vertical Modes and Horizontal Rays as well as 3D PE calculations are carried out to explain the experimental observations. [Work supported by ONR 322OA.]</jats:p>
title: Estimating waveguide parameters using horizontal and vertical arrays in the vicinity of horizontal Lloyd’s mirror in shallow water
